newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin raps Kremlin plots, gets military warning.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin raps Kremlin plots, gets military warning.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin ordered state officials on Friday to stop jostling for power as he faces heart surgery and promptly got a warning that "uncontrollable" upheaval looms among Russia's cash-starved military.

Yeltsin, sounding confident ahead of next month's planned heart surgery, told squabbling civilian leaders in a radio address to end Kremlin intrigue, making clear he plans to stay in office for his full four-year term.

But in a sign of daunting problems awaiting the elite, Defence Minister Igor Rodionov sounded the latest of several warnings from military chiefs. Without budget changes, he said Russia's cash-strapped army was on the brink of "uncontrollable developments".

Policy-makers also received a stinging rebuke from the International Monetary Fund, whose mission, worried about low tax collection, has left Moscow without agreeing to cough up more cash for Russia's market reforms.

"I want to remind the politicians -- Russia has made its choice for the next four years," Yeltsin said in a five-minute radio address apparently recorded in the Barvikha sanitorium where he is preparing for his heart bypass operation.
"There have been enough struggles for influence, fights for jobs, criticism and electioneering. It is time to work...
"While each player only plays his own pipe we will only be marking time and will lose the people's trust," Yeltsin said in a clear, confident voice.

His wife Naina told Russian public television on Thursday night that the workaholic Yeltsin was frustrated at not being able to carry out a full workload and was anxious to have his operation and get back to the Kremlin as soon as possible.
"He suffers because he cannot work at full force, that is a full working day from morning to night," she said.
A date for the operation has not been fixed but doctors, apparently satisfied with the president's overall condition, say it will probably take place in the latter half of November.

Rodionov's comments, reported by Interfax news agency, pinpointed the plight of Russia's once-powerful army after years of underfunding which have driven many soldiers to beg on the streets and forced officers to take other jobs.

"Russia's leadership and society should know that the chronic lack of funds are taking the armed forces to the brink of undesirable, and even uncontrollable, developments," Interfax quoted Rodionov as saying.

"If the 1997 defence budget is not changed, Russia may lose the armed forces as an integral and active state structure, with all the consequences which would follow that," he said, but gave no details.

Parliament has rejected the budget and ministers say a new draft being discussed this week will give more money to the military. But the budget deficit will stay the same and it is not clear where the money will come from.
Russia's former national security supremo, Alexander Lebed, sacked by President Boris Yeltsin last week, has warned that the armed forces were on the brink of rebellion.
Lebed's warning -- dismissed by Rodionov at the time -- gave a dramatic twist to a fierce battle for influence that has accompanied Yeltsin's prolonged absence from the Kremlin.
Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov accused the popular, gruff security chief of plotting to seize power by force.
Lebed, who hopes one day to become president, denied the accusations and has not been charged with any wrongdoing.
In Friday's radio address Yeltsin said such public scandals involving top officials harmed Russian democracy.
"Such actions discredit the (state) powers, they are undermining citizens' confidence in the state," he said.
